bibliography.checked_against: the first page (PDF p. 1: 'Ecology, 83(8), 2002, pp. 2145–2151') and Crossref
bibliography.note: D. Albrey Arrington, Kirk O. Winemiller, William F. Loftus, Senol Akin. Title printed 'How often do fishes "run on empty"?'.

claims.claim: across studies, 35 % of diurnal piscivores had empty stomachs, against 16 % of fishes as a whole
claims.location: p. 2149 (PDF p. 5), Results and discussion (Trophic classification); p. 2145 (PDF p. 1), Abstract; Table 2, p. 2148
claims.quote: was similar to that of our diurnal piscivores (35.2 Ϯ 3.5%; Table 2)
claims.conditions: species-level percentages of individuals with empty stomachs, averaged across species (mean ± 1 SE): diurnal piscivores 35.2 ± 3.5 % (50 species, Table 2) vs all fishes 16.2 ± 1.2 % (254 species, 36,875 individuals; species with ≥ 10 fish from one location, mean 145 per species); the authors' own diet collections from the Zambezi (Africa), Río Tortuguero and Orinoco basins (Central/South America) and Matagorda Bay, the Kissimmee River and the Everglades (Texas, Florida); all seasons, juveniles and adults pooled
claims.note: The digits and comparison hold. Precise wording: 'on average 35 % of a diurnal piscivore species' individuals had empty stomachs, against 16 % across 254 species'. 'Across studies' means across the authors' own pooled field collections (tropical and subtropical rivers, an estuary and Florida wetlands), not a literature review; no temperate lake is included. Engulfers (prey swallowed whole, e.g. largemouth bass) were empty significantly more often than biters, and species with extended parental care were over-represented among those empty > 50 % — both relevant to pickerel and smallmouth.

notes: Nocturnal fishes were empty more often (18.9 ± 2.2 %) than diurnal (15.4 ± 1.1 %); nocturnal piscivores less often than diurnal piscivores (Table 2). The authors note including juveniles probably understates piscivores' empty-stomach rate (ontogenetic diet shifts).
